# Diagnosing Weak Windshield Washer Jets on an Infiniti Q45

When both windshield washer jets on a 2002 Infiniti Q45 are delivering weak spray, dismissing it as a simple clog is a common diagnostic error. The owner manual explicitly notes that the jets contain built-in check valves designed to prevent fluid from draining back into the reservoir when the engine is off. While this feature protects the pump and seals, it introduces a specific failure mode that often confuses technicians: simultaneous blockage at both outlets. It is statistically improbable for debris to clog two separate nozzles with identical precision at the exact same moment, yet it happens frequently enough that "double clog" remains a primary suspect in these older chassis.

However, assuming the check valves are functioning correctly and the nozzles are clear requires looking upstream at the fluid dynamics of the system. The most probable cause for weak pressure on both sides is not a mechanical failure within the spray heads themselves, but rather a restriction or loss of volume in the supply line feeding them. In many vehicle architectures, including the Infiniti Q45 of this era, the pump does not push fluid directly to the jets; it pushes into a reservoir or a central manifold that then distributes the pressure via smaller diameter lines.

If you inspect the lines running from the pump to the firewall, you will often find a T-connector or a Y-splitter. Over time, mineral deposits from the washer fluid, combined with oxidized rubber seals at these connection points, can create a partial obstruction. If the restriction occurs just before the split, both jets suffer equally. This scenario mimics a pump failure because the pressure at the nozzle is low, even though the pump might still be moving fluid. To verify this, you must isolate the pump output. Disconnect the line from the firewall and direct the flow into a bucket or open space while actuating the washer switch. If the spray volume increases significantly at the source but remains weak at the jets, the issue is definitely in the distribution plumbing or the check valves within the nozzles are stuck closed due to pressure imbalance.

Another critical factor is the condition of the pump itself. The Infiniti Q45 utilizes a standard electric windshield washer pump located under the hood, often mounted near the firewall. These pumps rely on an impeller that spins against fluid resistance. If the fluid level in the reservoir is low, the impeller can run dry, leading to cavitation. Cavitation creates air bubbles that interrupt the hydraulic pressure required to force fluid through narrow nozzles. Even if the pump motor is spinning at full speed, a lack of prime volume results in sputtering output rather than a consistent stream. The check valves in the jets exacerbate this; if air enters the line due to low fluid levels, it gets trapped behind the one-way valves when the system pressurizes.

To resolve this without replacing expensive OEM parts immediately, you can attempt to clear the lines manually. Locate the small hose clamp at the firewall connection point. Loosen the clamp and pull the line back. Inspect the interior for visible debris or hardened washer fluid sludge. If the line is clear, try disconnecting the line from the pump side of the firewall connector and blowing compressed air through it (with the reservoir empty). This can dislodge partial blockages that are causing pressure drops.

If manual clearing fails, the check valves inside the nozzles may have failed mechanically. These valves are designed to allow flow in only one direction. If a valve seat corrodes or the internal spring fatigues, it can restrict flow regardless of pump pressure. Replacing the nozzle assemblies is often cheaper than replacing the entire washer system on this model. Before doing so, ensure you are using high-quality washer fluid; cheap fluids containing excessive wax or improper pH levels accelerate seal degradation and valve sticking.

Finally, consider the electrical aspect. A failing pump motor often shows a decrease in RPM under load. If the motor is struggling to maintain speed against the resistance of the check valves and narrow lines, the output pressure will drop. Measuring the voltage at the pump connector while operating the washer can reveal if the system is drawing excessive current, indicating a mechanical binding or an internal short within the motor windings. Addressing the fluid path integrity first usually resolves the issue, but electrical diagnostics are necessary if hydraulic checks yield no improvement.
